heading: Hill kingdoms of the Khasi, Garo and Jaintia
body: Meghalaya's history is not one history but three, run in parallel for centuries by the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo peoples across the plateau and hills between the Brahmaputra and Surma valleys. Each built its own political order rather than a single unified kingdom: the Khasi Hills were governed by a confederation of small syiemships (chieftaincies), the Jaintia kingdom by the 19th century controlled a swathe of hills and plains stretching into what is now Bangladesh, and the Garo Hills were organised around clan-based nokma leadership. All three societies share a matrilineal structure still practiced today, in which property and clan name pass through the mother's line — a social system rare in India and one that predates any written record of contact with the plains kingdoms or the British.

British control arrived late and by force. The Khasi chief U Tirot Sing led a four-year guerrilla resistance, the Anglo-Khasi War of 1829–1833, against East India Company plans to cut a road through his territory linking Assam to Sylhet; he was eventually captured and died in exile in 1835, the same year the Jaintia kingdom was formally annexed after its own armed resistance. The Garo Hills came under British administration only in the 1870s. For the following century the region was administered as hill districts of colonial, then independent, Assam.

Meghalaya was carved out of Assam as a separate state on 21 January 1972, under the North Eastern Areas Reorganisation Act, 1971 — a recognition of the hill districts' distinct tribal identity and Sixth Schedule autonomous status rather than of any historical unity among the Khasi, Jaintia and Garo themselves. The places mapped here sit inside that longer, plural history: the syiemships, the sites of resistance to British rule, and the institutions that carried Khasi, Jaintia and Garo self-government into the modern state.
